c.tagline: Where the Tigris meets 1,400 years of history.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used; fares are agreed with the driver upfront or set by common route, and shared 'service' taxis charge a fixed per-seat price.

emergency.medical: 122 (ambulance service is limited/unreliable; private hospitals or embassy contacts are often faster)
emergency.note: National emergency hotline 112; fire 115. Foreign visitors should also keep their embassy's emergency line on hand.

avoid.reason: Most governments advise against non-essential travel; in particular avoid Sadr City, protest gatherings, and movement outside secure areas after dark.
Use vetted drivers rather than street taxis, steer clear of demonstrations, checkpoints, and military convoys, and keep a low profile at all times.

hood_desc: Baghdad's buzzing commercial and dining hub on a bend of the Tigris, packed with markets, cafes and mid-range hotels; a walkable, comparatively relaxed base for first-time visitors.

Home to the fortified International (Green) Zone with government buildings, embassies and the city's most secure five-star hotels; suited to diplomats, journalists and business travelers who prioritize security.
An upscale, leafy shopping and residential district with malls, embassies and modern restaurants; popular with expatriates, NGO staff and diaspora Iraqis visiting family.
A quieter university peninsula wrapped by the Tigris, home to the University of Baghdad and tree-lined streets; a calmer choice for academics and longer-stay visitors.
The historic east-bank core around Rashid Street and Mutanabbi Street, dense with old markets, bookshops and budget hotels; best for culture-focused travelers wanting old-city atmosphere.
lodging: Al Harithiya House for Hotel Apartments

water.note: Infrastructure and contamination issues make tap water unsuitable for drinking; use bottled water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver; there is no rechargeable transit card. Shared 'service' taxis running fixed routes are far more common than public buses and are paid per seat in dinars.
transit.hours: Public buses and shared taxis generally run roughly 6am-10pm; after that, private taxis or ride-hailing apps are the only options.
transit.note: Public transit is minimal and unreliable; most residents and visitors rely on private cars, shared service taxis, or ride-hailing apps. A metro system is under construction with completion targeted around 2029.

train: Iraqi Republic Railways (limited domestic services to Basra, Mosul and Fallujah from Baghdad Central Station)
bus: Intercity buses/shared taxis from Baghdad's Nahda and Alawi garages to Basra, Erbil, Najaf and Karbala

airport.name: Baghdad International Airport (BGW)
airport.drive: 25-40 min depending on traffic and security checkpoints

transit.m: No public bus/metro serves the airport

tip.r: Not traditionally required, but rounding up taxi fares and leaving 5-10% at upscale restaurants and hotels is appreciated.
